questions.question: In the standard lifecycle of a ServiceNow incident, which state generally follows 'In Progress' when the agent is waiting for information from the requester?

choices.text: Resolved
On Hold
Closed
Canceled

questions.explanation: The 'On Hold' state is used when resolution is paused while waiting for an external action (e.g. a response from the requester), along with an associated 'Hold reason'.
pieges: Confusing 'On Hold' with 'Resolved', which means the issue has already been addressed.

questions.question: How is an incident's priority generally determined in a standard ServiceNow configuration?

choices.text: It is entered freely by the end user
It results from an Impact x Urgency matrix
It is always equal to the urgency
It depends solely on the assignment group

questions.explanation: Priority is automatically calculated via a priority matrix crossing Impact and Urgency, which is configurable in the system.
pieges: Believing that priority is a free-text field manually entered by default.

questions.question: What is the main difference between 'Assignment group' and 'Assigned to' on an incident?

choices.text: They are two names for the same field
Assignment group designates the responsible team, Assigned to designates the specific person
Assigned to is mandatory, Assignment group is optional
Assignment group only applies to Problems

questions.explanation: 'Assignment group' identifies the team/group in charge, while 'Assigned to' identifies the specific individual within (or outside of) that group.
pieges: Thinking that filling in Assigned to removes the need to define Assignment group in a standard routing process.

questions.question: Which record is used to document the root cause linked to one or more incidents?

choices.text: Change Request
Problem
Knowledge Article
Service Catalog Request

questions.explanation: Problem Management aims to identify and document the root cause, whereas Incident Management aims for rapid restoration of service.
pieges: Confusing Incident (symptom, rapid restoration) with Problem (root cause).

questions.question: What typically happens when an incident in the 'Resolved' state is reopened by a user?

choices.text: Nothing, the 'Reopen count' field does not exist
The 'Reopen count' field is incremented
The incident is automatically closed (Closed)
A new Problem is automatically created

questions.explanation: The 'Reopen count' field is incremented every time a previously Resolved/Closed incident is reopened, which is useful as a quality tracking indicator.
pieges: Forgetting this field exists and serves as a resolution quality indicator.

questions.question: A major incident affecting multiple users often generates several individual incidents. How are they generally organized?

choices.text: They are automatically merged into a single record
They are attached as 'child incidents' to a parent incident
They are deleted in favor of the Problem only
They cannot be linked together

questions.explanation: The Major Incident process links similar individual incidents as children of a parent incident, to centralize communication and resolution.
pieges: Thinking that a major incident requires grouping everything into a single Problem from the outset.

questions.question: What is the distinction between an SLA and an OLA?

choices.text: None, they are synonyms
The SLA is a commitment to the customer, the OLA is an internal agreement between teams
The OLA only applies to Changes
The SLA only applies to Problems

questions.explanation: The SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a time commitment generally made to the customer/business, while the OLA (Operational Level Agreement) is an equivalent agreement between internal teams.
pieges: Confusing the two terms which, although mechanically similar, have a different contractual scope.

questions.question: An incident moves from 'New' directly to 'Resolved' without ever going through 'In Progress'. Is this a problem by default in ServiceNow?

choices.text: No, state transitions are not restricted by default unless a specific configuration exists (e.g. a state flow policy)
Yes, this is technically impossible natively
Yes, this automatically deletes the incident
No, but it permanently locks the incident

questions.explanation: By default, ServiceNow does not enforce a strict order of transitions between states unless a state transition policy (State Flow / UI Policy / Business Rule) is explicitly configured to enforce it.
pieges: Wrongly assuming that a transition order is locked natively without additional configuration.

questions.question: Which field indicates the extent of an incident's effect on the business (e.g. a single user vs the whole company)?

choices.text: Urgency
Impact
Priority
Severity

questions.explanation: 'Impact' measures the extent of the effect on the business, while 'Urgency' measures how quickly a resolution is needed.
pieges: Swapping Impact and Urgency in their respective definitions.

questions.question: Why doesn't a 'Resolved' incident move immediately to 'Closed'?

choices.text: Because they are technically the same state
To allow a confirmation period before automatic/manual closure
Because 'Closed' does not exist in Incident Management
Because a Problem must first be created

questions.explanation: A common practice is to leave an incident in 'Resolved' for a defined period, allowing the requester to reopen it if needed, before automatic closure.
pieges: Believing that Resolved and Closed are interchangeable and have no functional distinction.

questions.question: Which type of record can be created from an incident to request a configuration change in order to permanently fix the cause of a recurring problem?

choices.text: A Knowledge Article
A Change Request
A Catalog Item
An Update Set

questions.explanation: A Change Request is used to implement a controlled modification aimed at permanently fixing an identified root cause, often linked to a Problem.
pieges: Forgetting the logical link Incident → Problem → Change when handling root causes.

questions.question: An agent wants to document a reusable workaround for a recurring incident. Which type of record is best suited to capture this information?

choices.text: A Knowledge Article
A new duplicate incident
A Catalog Item
An Update Set

questions.explanation: A Knowledge Article captures a solution or workaround so it can be reused by other agents or in self-service.
pieges: Duplicating the incident instead of creating a reusable knowledge article.

questions.question: In what order does ServiceNow evaluate ACLs when attempting to access a specific field on a table?

choices.text: Field ACL then table ACL
Table ACL then field ACL
Both simultaneously with no defined order
Only the field ACL, the table ACL is ignored

questions.explanation: ServiceNow first checks the table-level ACL for the requested operation; if it fails, the field ACL is not even evaluated.
pieges: Confusing the evaluation order of table ACL vs field ACL.

questions.question: An ACL has no role specified, no condition, and no script. What is the resulting behavior?

choices.text: No one has access
Only admins have access
Any authenticated user reaching this ACL has access
The ACL is ignored and a system error is raised

questions.explanation: An ACL with no restrictive criteria (no role, no condition, no script) grants access to any authenticated user — a classic security pitfall to watch for.
pieges: Forgetting that an 'empty' ACL is permissive by default, not restrictive.

questions.question: A Client Script hides a button from an unauthorized user. Is this enough to secure the action server-side?

choices.text: Yes, hiding the button is enough
No, real security must be enforced via server-side ACLs
Yes, if the Client Script is marked 'Isolate script'
No, the Client Script must be completely disabled

questions.explanation: A Client Script runs in the browser and can be bypassed; effective security must always be guaranteed server-side via ACLs.
pieges: Believing that a Client Script constitutes reliable security.

questions.question: Which role is generally required (with role elevation) to modify the ACLs themselves in a standard instance?

choices.text: itil
catalog_admin
security_admin
approver_user

questions.explanation: The 'security_admin' role, combined with role elevation (Elevate Roles), is required by default to modify ACL records.
pieges: Thinking that the 'admin' role alone is enough without explicit security role elevation.

questions.question: A table-level read ACL fails for a user. What happens to the field ACLs associated with that same table?

choices.text: They are evaluated independently regardless
They are never reached because access is already denied at the table level
They automatically become permissive
They only apply to admins

questions.explanation: If the table ACL fails, the user has no access to the record anyway, so the field ACLs are not relevant/reached.
pieges: Forgetting the hierarchical dependency between table ACLs and field ACLs.

questions.question: Which type of ACL specifically protects the calling of a Script Include from the client (client-callable)?

choices.text: A classic table ACL
An ACL of type 'record'
An ACL of type 'client_callable' / script
There is no ACL for this

questions.explanation: Script Includes marked 'Client callable' can be protected by a dedicated script-type ACL to control who can invoke them from the client.
pieges: Believing that checking 'Client callable' alone is enough without thinking about securing the call.

questions.question: Which distinct operations can a table ACL typically control?

choices.text: Only read
create, read, write, delete
Only write and delete
Only access to the UI module

questions.explanation: Table ACLs can be defined separately for create, read, write, and delete, each with its own conditions/roles.
pieges: Thinking that a single ACL covers all CRUD operations for a table.

questions.question: Does a user with the admin role automatically have access to all data, regardless of the ACLs?

choices.text: Always yes, admin bypasses everything
Not necessarily: it depends on the 'Admin overrides' configuration and the ACLs themselves
No, admin never has more access than a standard user
Yes, but only for system tables

questions.explanation: Admin access depends on the ACL configuration and system properties such as 'Admin overrides' — it is not an automatic, unconditional bypass.
pieges: Assuming that the admin role guarantees full access regardless of the ACL configuration.

questions.question: What does an Update Set primarily capture?

choices.text: Business data created by users (e.g. incidents)
Configuration/customization changes made to the instance
System logs
Full database backups

questions.explanation: An Update Set captures configuration changes (fields, forms, scripts, etc.), not business data created by users.
pieges: Believing that an Update Set migrates data (records): it only migrates configuration.

questions.question: What must be done before starting development so that changes are properly isolated?

choices.text: Nothing, all changes automatically go into a dedicated Update Set
Set the desired Update Set as 'Current'
Delete the Default Update Set
Activate the security_admin role

questions.explanation: You must explicitly set the working Update Set as 'Current' so that changes are captured in it, otherwise they go into the Default set.
pieges: Forgetting to set the correct Update Set as 'Current' before starting development.

questions.question: Which step is recommended before committing a Retrieved Update Set on a target instance?

choices.text: Commit it directly without checking
Do a Preview to detect conflicts (collisions)
Mark it Ignored
Rename it

questions.explanation: The Preview lets you identify potential conflicts ('collisions') between the Update Set and the current state of the target instance before committing.
pieges: Committing an Update Set without a prior Preview, thereby missing conflicts.

questions.question: An Update Set is marked 'Complete'. What should be done if additional changes are needed?

choices.text: Reopen and modify this Update Set directly
Create a new Update Set for the additional changes
Delete the completed Update Set and redo everything
Set the instance to read-only

questions.explanation: Once 'Complete', an Update Set should no longer be modified; additional changes should go into a new Update Set.
pieges: Reopening and modifying an Update Set already marked Complete, which can create inconsistencies.

questions.question: Several Update Sets have dependencies on each other (one requires fields created by the other). Why does the commit order matter?

choices.text: It never matters, ServiceNow reorders automatically
Committing in the wrong order can cause errors or missing references
Only the last committed Update Set matters
The order only affects performance, never functionality

questions.explanation: If an Update Set depends on elements created by another one, they must be committed in the right order or errors/broken references can occur.
pieges: Ignoring dependencies between Update Sets during multiple migrations.

questions.question: A developer is working within a scoped application. Where are their configuration changes captured?

choices.text: Always only in the Global Update Set
In the current Update Set, within the context of the application's scope
Nowhere, scoped apps don't use Update Sets
Only via a manual XML export

questions.explanation: Changes are captured in the current Update Set, with the context of the active scoped application, just like for global development.
pieges: Believing that scoped applications entirely bypass the Update Set mechanism.

questions.question: What is the main risk of leaving the Default Update Set as 'Current' during structured development?

choices.text: No particular risk
Mixing unrelated changes together, making a clean, targeted migration difficult
It automatically locks the instance
It deletes existing data

questions.explanation: Working in the Default set mixes all changes indiscriminately, which greatly complicates a clean, selective migration to other instances.
pieges: Underestimating the impact of the disorder created by extended use of the Default Update Set.

questions.question: When does a 'before' Business Rule run relative to the database write?

choices.text: After the write
Before the write, and it can modify or cancel the operation
In parallel, asynchronously
Only when the form loads

questions.explanation: A 'before' Business Rule runs before the record is written to the database, allowing values to be changed or the operation to be aborted (abortInsert/abortAction).
pieges: Confusing 'before' and 'after': modifying current in an 'after' rule does not prevent the write that has already occurred.

questions.question: Which type of Business Rule is best suited to send an external notification without blocking the user?

choices.text: before
display
async
on submit

questions.explanation: An 'async' Business Rule runs asynchronously after the write, ideal for non-blocking actions such as external calls or heavy notifications.
pieges: Using a blocking 'before' rule for an action that could slow down the save.

questions.question: When does an 'onLoad' Client Script run?

choices.text: When a field changes
When the form loads
When the form is submitted
During inline editing in a list

questions.explanation: 'onLoad' runs when the form is loaded in the browser, before any user interaction.
pieges: Confusing onLoad with onChange, which fires when a specific field is modified.

questions.question: Which type of Client Script can prevent a form from being submitted if a condition is not met?

choices.text: onLoad
onChange
onSubmit
onCellEdit

questions.explanation: 'onSubmit' runs on submission and can return false to block the submission of the form.
pieges: Trying to block a submission from an onLoad script, which runs too early for that.

questions.question: Why is a UI Policy often preferred over a Client Script to make a field mandatory based on a condition?

choices.text: UI Policies are faster to write in JavaScript
UI Policies are declarative, code-free, and simpler to maintain for this case
Client Scripts cannot make a field mandatory
There is no practical difference

questions.explanation: UI Policies let you define mandatory/visible/read-only declaratively without writing a script, reducing maintenance complexity for simple cases.
pieges: Writing a complex Client Script when a UI Policy would be enough.

questions.question: What is a 'display' Business Rule mainly used for?

choices.text: Running code after a record is deleted
Transferring data from the server to the client when the form loads
Blocking form submission
Modifying related records asynchronously

questions.explanation: A 'display' Business Rule runs when the form loads to transfer server-side calculated data to the client (then accessible via g_scratchpad, for example).
pieges: Confusing 'display' with before/after rules, which run during write operations.

questions.question: What does the 'Order' field determine on a Business Rule or Client Script?

choices.text: The display priority in lists
The relative execution order among rules/scripts of the same type
The role required to run it
The table the script applies to

questions.explanation: The 'Order' field determines in what order multiple rules or scripts of the same type applied to the same event run.
pieges: Assuming the execution order is purely random or based on the creation date.

questions.question: Why should a critical security validation never rely solely on a Client Script?

choices.text: Because Client Scripts are slow
Because a user can bypass the code running in their browser
Because Client Scripts cannot access fields
Because it consumes too many licenses

questions.explanation: Code running in the browser can be inspected or bypassed by the user; critical validation must be duplicated server-side (Business Rule/ACL).
pieges: Relying on client-side validation alone for a critical business rule.

questions.question: Which record is created when a user orders a standard Catalog Item from the cart?

choices.text: A Change Request
A Requested Item (RITM) attached to a Request (REQ)
An Incident
An Update Set

questions.explanation: Submitting a standard order generates a Request (REQ) containing one or more Requested Items (RITM), which drive the fulfillment workflow.
pieges: Forgetting the distinction between the overall Request and the individual Requested Items.

questions.question: How does a Record Producer differ from a standard Catalog Item?

choices.text: There is no difference
It creates a record directly in another table, without generating a RITM
It cannot have variables
It can only be used by admins

questions.explanation: A Record Producer creates a target record directly (e.g. an incident) from the entered data, without going through the standard RITM process.
pieges: Confusing Record Producer and Catalog Item: the Record Producer does not create a RITM.

questions.question: What is an Order Guide used for in the Service Catalog?

choices.text: To configure the variables of a single item
To allow ordering several related Catalog Items at once
To replace Catalog Client Scripts
To manage approvals only

questions.explanation: An Order Guide groups several Catalog Items that can be ordered together (e.g. full equipment kit for a new employee).
pieges: Forgetting that an Order Guide is used to group items, not to configure a single one in more detail.

questions.question: Which element lets you group reusable variables across several Catalog Items?

choices.text: A Variable Set
An Order Guide
A Catalog UI Policy
A Workflow

questions.explanation: A Variable Set groups a set of reusable variables that can be applied to several Catalog Items without redefining them each time.
pieges: Confusing Variable Set (grouping of fields) with Order Guide (grouping of items).

questions.question: When does the Workflow (or Flow Designer flow) associated with a Catalog Item trigger?

choices.text: As soon as the item is added to the cart
When the order is submitted (checkout)
Only upon manual approval by an admin
Never automatically, it must be started manually

questions.explanation: The associated Workflow/Flow triggers when the order is actually submitted (checkout), not simply when the item is added to the cart.
pieges: Thinking the Workflow/Flow triggers when the item is added to the cart rather than on submission.

questions.question: What does it mean for a Catalog Client Script to be marked 'Isolate script'?

choices.text: It runs in an isolated environment (Jelly scope), with limited access to the global DOM
It never runs on the client
It automatically becomes a Business Rule
It disables all other variables on the form

questions.explanation: The 'Isolate script' option runs the script in an isolated scope, limiting direct access to the global DOM, which improves robustness but may require adjustments for certain direct DOM manipulations.
pieges: Ignoring the impact of isolation on scripts that directly manipulate the DOM.

questions.question: Which type of record typically manages the approval steps generated when an order requires validation?

choices.text: sysapproval_approver
sys_user_group
kb_knowledge
sys_update_set

questions.explanation: Records in the sysapproval_approver table represent the individual approval steps generated by the request's workflow.
pieges: Confusing approval records with the user groups themselves.

questions.question: What does a Catalog UI Policy let you do with a Catalog Item's variables?

choices.text: Modify the database schema
Control the visibility/mandatory status of a variable based on the value of another, without scripting
Automatically create an Update Set
Generate a Knowledge Article

questions.explanation: A Catalog UI Policy declaratively lets you show/hide or make mandatory a variable depending on the value of another variable on the form.
pieges: Writing a complex Catalog Client Script for a case the Catalog UI Policy would cover natively.

questions.question: As part of the Incident Management process on ServiceNow, which specific action is associated with managing 'Major Incidents'?

choices.text: Using the Major Incident Workbench and the dedicated dashboard to oversee resolution.
Automatically promoting every priority 1 incident to a Major Incident without manual intervention.
Using exclusively the Known Error Portal to identify the root cause before declaring the incident major.
Restoring services only through agentic AI automation with no possibility of human intervention.

questions.explanation: The official documentation specifies that managing major incidents specifically involves creating these incidents and using the overview dashboard as well as the dedicated 'workbench' to track and manage the situation.
pieges: Believing that promotion to Major Incident is an entirely automatic process with no oversight.
Confusing major incident management with simply searching the Known Error Portal, which is a separate resource.
Thinking that agentic AI is the only tool allowed to manage major incidents, when it is actually a complementary automation option.

questions.question: In the context of ServiceNow, what is the fundamental distinction between a Business Rule and a Client Script according to platform best practices?

choices.text: Business Rules run on the server, while Client Scripts run in the user's browser.
Business Rules are used to manipulate the user interface, while Client Scripts handle database operations.
Business Rules can only run when a record is deleted, unlike Client Scripts which handle insertion.
Business Rules are obsolete and must be replaced by Client Scripts for all new automations.

questions.explanation: Business Rules are server-side scripts that fire during database operations (insert, update, delete, display, or query). Conversely, Client Scripts run client-side (in the browser) to interact with the form or the user interface.
pieges: Confusing where the code runs (server vs client).
Thinking that Business Rules are used to modify the user interface (like making a field mandatory), which is the role of Client Scripts.
Believing that Business Rules have been fully replaced by Client Scripts, when they are two complementary tools with distinct roles.

questions.question: In the context of security management on ServiceNow, what is the main role of an Access Control List (ACL)?

choices.text: Defining user roles at the global instance level only.
Restricting access to data by requiring users to meet specific conditions.
Automating the creation of user accounts for new integrations.
Encrypting sensitive data stored in database tables.

questions.explanation: ACLs (Access Control Lists) are ServiceNow's central security mechanism for controlling access to data. They impose requirements (roles, conditions, scripts) that a user must meet to interact with a given resource.
pieges: Confusing ACLs with role management (User Administration), which defines 'who' the user is, whereas ACLs define 'what they can do' with the data.
Thinking that ACLs are used for data encryption, which is a different function handled by other security modules.
Believing that ACLs only apply at the global instance level, when they are granular and can apply to specific tables or fields.

questions.question: When an ACL (Access Control List) contains multiple conditions (required roles, security attributes, data conditions, and scripts), what rule governs access to the object?

choices.text: The user must satisfy at least one of the specified conditions to gain access.
The user must satisfy all the conditions listed in the ACL to gain access.
The system evaluates the conditions sequentially and grants access as soon as one condition is met.
Access is granted by default if at least one data condition evaluates to true, regardless of roles.

questions.explanation: According to the documentation, if an ACL specifies multiple conditions, the user must satisfy all of them (roles, security attributes, data conditions, and scripts) to gain access to the object and the operation in question. Failing any one of these conditions results in access being denied.
pieges: Believing that an 'OR' relationship applies between the different types of conditions within the same ACL.
Thinking that the script is optional and not taken into account if the roles are already satisfied.
Confusing the evaluation of conditions within a single ACL with the sequential evaluation of multiple different ACLs.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of using 'Update Sets' in a ServiceNow instance?

choices.text: Backing up all transactional data and incidents to transfer them to a production instance.
Grouping a series of configuration changes to move them as a single unit to another instance.
Automating user account creation and role assignment between development and test instances.
Synchronizing operating system security updates for the server infrastructure hosting ServiceNow.

questions.explanation: An 'Update Set' is a transport mechanism specifically designed to move configuration changes (settings, flows, forms, etc.) between instances. It does not capture transactional data (such as tickets or users) by default.
pieges: Believing that Update Sets are used to migrate business data or transactions.
Confusing Update Sets with system update (patching) tools managed by ServiceNow at the infrastructure level.
Thinking that Update Sets automatically synchronize user accounts.

questions.question: A ServiceNow administrator wants to make sure users can see their requests and approvals on the catalog home page in the Service Portal. Which ServiceNow platform configuration determines the items displayed in the 'Requests and Approvals' widget?

choices.text: The 'My Request Filter' module in the platform.
The configuration of 'Catalog Categories' (sc_category).
Activating the 'Service Portal - Service Catalog v2' plugin.
Defining 'Saved Bundles' in the user profile.

questions.explanation: The source content explicitly states that the 'Requests and Approvals' widget displays a list based on the configurations available in the 'My Request Filter' module within the platform.
pieges: Confusing the request filter configuration with simply activating the plugin.
Thinking that approvals are managed directly via catalog categories instead of platform filters.
Believing that 'Saved Bundles' influence the visibility of approvals.

questions.question: When configuring Service Catalog categories, which condition is mandatory for a category to be visible to users in the catalog?

choices.text: The category must be defined as a root category with no parent.
The category must contain at least one active item within its hierarchy.
The user must have the catalog_admin role to see the category.
The category must be associated with a specific Workflow to be published.

questions.explanation: According to the documentation, if a category and its hierarchy contain no active items, the category does not appear in the catalog and cannot be added to it. Having at least one active item is therefore a prerequisite for it to display.
pieges: Believing that categories are visible as soon as they are created, even if empty.
Thinking that only administrators can see categories, when it is actually a matter of active content and availability settings.
Confusing visibility with roles (the admin or catalog_admin role is needed for configuration, but visibility is governed by the presence of active items).
